$$

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}$ is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}\,]=\sqrt{\frac{\text{MSE}}{{S}_{xx}}}
$$

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}

$$

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

$$

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$

$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

$$

In cases like this, the random variable

$$
\frac{\overset{―}{X}-\mu }{S/\sqrt{n}}
$$

can be approximated by the student's $t$-distribution ${T}_{n-1}$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom, where  

- $\overset{―}{X}$ is the sample mean,

- $\mu$ is the population mean,

- ${S}^{2}$ is the sample variance, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\overset{―}{x}\pm {t}_{n-1,\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}},
$$

where $P(T>{t}_{n-1,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ and $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

In our case,

$$
\overset{―}{x}=32.5\,\text{mpg},\,n=49,\,s=4.2\,\text{mpg}.
$$
